name: EU Company → US Expansion
overview: Expanding a European company into the United States presents a mirror image of the challenges European subsidiaries face when acquired by US companies, but viewed from the other side. The single biggest shock for European employers is at-will employment — the US has no statutory notice periods, no requirement for cause to terminate, and no mandatory severance. A European manager used to 3-month notice periods and works council consultation will find they can (and are expected to) terminate underperformers in days. However, this flexibility is balanced by significant litigation risk: US employment lawsuits are common, expensive, and often decided by juries. The US has no mandatory paid vacation, no federal paid sick leave, and a healthcare system tied to employment — a benefit European employers rarely need to provide. Compensation culture is different: higher base salaries, equity is expected at tech companies, and benefits (health, dental, vision, 401k matching) are a core part of the package. The US is not one labor market but 50 — state laws on minimum wage, paid leave, non-competes, and pay equity vary widely. Most European companies enter through Delaware (for incorporation) and start operations in New York, California, Texas, or Massachusetts.

entity_types.recommended: Delaware C-Corporation (most common for VC-backed and tech companies; preferred by investors for well-established corporate law and Court of Chancery).
alternatives: Delaware LLC (pass-through taxation, simpler but less familiar to US investors; not ideal if seeking venture capital)
New York or California corporation (if primarily operating in one state initially — avoid double registration complexity)
S-Corporation (not available to non-US residents as shareholders — check shareholder structure)

legal_requirements: Incorporate in Delaware (most common) or the target operating state. File with Secretary of State, obtain EIN from IRS, register for state taxes.
Foreign qualification: If incorporating in Delaware but operating in another state (e.g., California), register as a foreign entity in that state — non-compliance triggers back taxes and penalties.
Federal EIN (Employer Identification Number) required for tax withholding, banking, and hiring. Obtain via IRS Form SS-4.
State-level registration for unemployment insurance tax (SUTA) and workers' compensation insurance — each state has a separate process.
New York: Register with NY Department of Labor for withholding; file New York Certificate of Authority for foreign entities; NYC has additional requirements (human rights law, paid safe/sick leave).

California: EDD (Employment Development Department) registration for payroll taxes; mandatory paid sick leave (minimum 40 hours per year for most employees); Cal-OSHA compliance; stringent pay data reporting (pay equity) for companies with 100+ employees.
Massachusetts: Paid family and medical leave (PFML) contributions mandatory; strict non-compete law (non-competes only enforceable with new consideration and limited to 12 months).
Federal: I-9 employment eligibility verification for all hires; E-Verify (mandatory in some states, federal contractors); W-4 and W-2 compliance.

Federal: FLSA (Fair Labor Standards Act) compliance — distinguish exempt (salaried, overtime-exempt) vs non-exempt (hourly, overtime-eligible) employees; minimum wage at federal level is $7.25 but state rates are higher (NY $15-16, CA $16, MA $15).

Immigration: L-1 visa for intracompany transferees (managerial, executive, or specialized knowledge) — requires qualifying relationship between EU entity and US entity; H-1B visa for specialty occupations (annual lottery, ~20-30% chance); E-2 treaty investor visa available for nationals of certain EU countries (Germany, UK, France, Italy, Netherlands, etc.) but requires substantial investment and no path to permanent residence.
ACA (Affordable Care Act) compliance: employers with 50+ full-time equivalents must offer minimum essential health coverage or face penalties (play-or-pay mandate).

State paid leave programs: New York (PFL), California (CFRA/PDL), Massachusetts (PFML), Washington (PFML), and others require employee-funded leave programs for family and medical leave. These are not optional and carry specific contribution rates.

hiring_timeline.phase_1: Founding team entry (month 1-3): Founders enter on ESTA/Visa Waiver or B-1 visa (for business activities, not productive work). Incorporate in Delaware. Open US bank account. Register for EIN. Use PEO/EOR (e.g., Rippling, TriNet, Justworks) for first US hires.
hiring_timeline.phase_2: First US hires and office (month 3-8): Transition from PEO to direct employment. Hire US-based leadership (US country manager, sales lead, or general counsel). Lease office space (if not remote-first). Set up US health insurance, 401k plan. Register in applicable states.
hiring_timeline.phase_3: Scale US operations (month 6-18): Build US team to 10-50+ employees. Consider establishing additional offices in other states. Implement US-style HR policies (performance reviews, PIPs, equity administration). Transition from EU-style management to US norms.

org_structure_adaptations: US subsidiary typically operates with more autonomy from European HQ than European subs receive — geographical distance and cultural differences demand more delegation
At-will employment means the US arm can hire/fire faster. European HQs often struggle to accept local management's recommendation to terminate someone on the basis of performance alone.
Add a US General Counsel or employment lawyer relationship from day one — employment litigation risk is much higher than in Europe
US entity needs a board (even if minimal) with at least one US-resident director; many European companies appoint a local advisory board for credibility
Equity compensation requires a US equity plan and 409A valuation (independent appraisal of common stock value) — costly but necessary
Head of People/HR function in the US needs US-specific expertise (benefits administration, compliance, state law complexity) — European HR generalists may lack this knowledge
compensation_notes: US compensation is higher than Europe in most professional roles, particularly in tech hubs (San Francisco, New York, Seattle, Boston, Austin). Base salaries are typically 20-50% higher than equivalent European roles. Equity compensation (stock options or RSUs) is standard at growth-stage tech companies and increasingly expected even at smaller startups. Total compensation benchmarking is critical — use Radford, Option Impact, or Pave surveys. Benefits are a major differentiator: health insurance (medical, dental, vision) costs $8-15k per employee annually (employer typically covers 70-85%). 401(k) matching (3-6% typical) is expected. There is no statutory holiday minimum (zero mandatory vacation days), but competitive companies offer 15-25 days PTO plus 10-11 federal holidays. Paid parental leave is increasingly common but not federally mandated — competitive companies offer 12-20 weeks. Performance bonuses (10-30% of base) are standard in professional services and sales. Sales commission structures are formulaic and transparent (vs. more discretionary in Europe). Overtime pay (1.5x for non-exempt employees over 40 hours/week) must be tracked. Pay equity laws in several states require proactive reporting and analysis.
cultural_key_differences: At-will employment is shocking to Europeans — no notice period, no cause requirement, no works council. This is normal in the US and not indicative of a hostile work environment.

Work hours are longer in the US than in Europe. 50+ hour weeks are common in professional services and tech. Taking all your vacation is less common — there is a 'hustle culture' that values visible effort.

Direct communication: US managers give direct, candid feedback. PIPs (Performance Improvement Plans) are genuine termination processes, not improvement tools. This contrasts with Europe's longer coaching culture.
Healthcare is tied to employment. Europeans used to universal healthcare find this jarring. Explaining health insurance options during onboarding is a critical HR function.

Individualism: US workplace culture values individual achievement, self-promotion, and taking credit. This can seem arrogant to Europeans. Employees are expected to advocate for themselves in reviews and promotion cycles.

Customer service orientation: US culture emphasizes friendliness and enthusiasm in customer-facing roles. 'Have a great day' is genuine, not sarcastic. European directness can come across as rudeness.
Litigation culture: US employees are more likely to sue. Every HR decision (hiring, firing, promotion, compensation) must be defensible on non-discriminatory grounds. Documentation is critical.

Diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) is a central HR focus in US companies. European companies expanding to the US should prepare for expectations around DEI programs, reporting, and transparency that may exceed European norms.
Regional cultural differences are significant: New York is fast-paced and direct; San Francisco is more relaxed and informal; Boston is formal and academic; Texas is polite and relationship-oriented.
common_pitfalls: Not budgeting for healthcare costs. US health insurance is $8-15k per employee annually. A team of 20 employees adds $160-300k in benefits cost alone.

Assuming non-compete agreements from Europe are enforceable in the US. Non-compete enforcement varies wildly by state (banned in California, Oklahoma, North Dakota; restricted in many others post-FTC 2024 rule).
Underestimating state-level compliance. Operating in 5 states means 5 sets of payroll tax registrations, 5 unemployment insurance systems, 5 sets of paid leave laws, and potentially 5 minimum wages.
Treating the entire US like one market. New York success does not predict Texas success. California regulations differ significantly from Florida or Georgia.
Failing to provide sexual harassment prevention training. Several states (CA, NY, CT, DE, IL) mandate annual or biennial training for all employees. Non-compliance carries fines.
Not having an at-will disclaimer in the employee handbook. Without explicit at-will language, courts may imply contractual employment rights — exactly what at-will is supposed to avoid.

Ignoring W-2 vs W-9 (1099) classification. Worker misclassification is aggressively enforced by the IRS and state agencies (California's Dynamex test is the strictest). Penalties include back taxes, interest, and fines.

Overlooking state paid family leave contributions. In New York, California, Massachusetts, and others, employers must deduct and remit contributions for paid leave programs. These are not optional opt-ins.

Assuming European employment documentation (contracts, handbooks) is sufficient for the US. US handbooks must cover: at-will employment, EEO/anti-discrimination policy, harassment policy, leave policies, code of conduct, confidentiality, and disclaimer language.

Not engaging US immigration counsel early enough. The H-1B lottery runs once a year (March). L-1 requires the US entity to already exist and have office space. Timing mismanagement frequently delays key intracompany transfers by 6-12 months.
timeline_estimate: 6-18 months for full US operational setup. Delaware incorporation: 1-2 weeks. EIN and bank account: 2-4 weeks. First hires via PEO: 1-2 months. Transition to direct employment: 3-6 months. Full compliance infrastructure (multi-state): 6-12 months.
